messages.author: 833479854a80815e
messages.subject: implement non-stationarity
parts:
Dear all, 
I implemented a non-stationary spde model the following way:

spde.nonstat<-inla.spde2.matern(mesh, B.tau=cbind(0, 0, 0, 1, values_on_mesh), 
                                B.kappa=cbind(0, 1, values_on_mesh, 0, 0),
                                theta.prior.mean=rep(0,4),
                                theta.prior.prec=rep(1,4))

and I wonder if this is correct, as the internal representation in INLA is theta_1=log(tau) and theta_2=log(kappa) and in my opinion this is not coherent with how I did it, which is
log(tau)=theta_3+ values_on_mesh*theta_4
log(kappa)=theta_1+values_on_mesh*theta_2.

Looking forward to your help. Thank you.

Corinna

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] implement non-stationarity
parts:
The internal representation is only theta_1=log(tau) when B.tau =
cbind(0, 1, 0); the internal representation is _defined_ by the
user-supplied B.tau and B.kappa matrices. Your representation is
precisely the intended way to extend this model to non-stationarity.
See the Details section of ?inla.spde2.matern, which defines the exact
construction. The inla.spde.result() method uses the B-matrices to
compute the nominal range and variance (or the log() of them) also in
the non-stationary case.
However, the tau&kappa parameterisation isn't the ideal way to
represent nonstationarity since it's hard to control the variance
behaviour (it depends on both kappa and tau), and there are several
solutions to this. One can be implemented using the existing
inla.spde2.matern function, but the best solution will require a new
internal model, that we're working on.

For the inla.spde2.matern() interface, there is a better way to
parameterise the existing implementation to get at least partial
separation between range and variance; using the approach from the
2015 JSS paper that uses "nominal range" and "nominal standard
deviation" as the basis for the parameterisation isn't perfect in the
non-stationary case, but it should be more well behaved than the pure
tau/kappa parameterisation. See pages 4-6 fo
https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v063i19 that includes the
derivation of the needed B.tau and B.kappa parameters.

Of course, using a non-stationary extension of the PC-prior model for
the covariance parameters would be preferable, and that's part of what
one of my PhD students is currently working on.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] implement non-stationarity
parts:
The b_k(tau) = -b_k(kappa) part is needed if one wants to control the
range separately from the marginal variance. Both approaches give
"valid" models, but the interpretation and properties are different.
This is because in the basic (kappa^2 - Delta)^{alpha/2} (tau x) = W
model, the marginal variance is proportional to 1/(kappa^{2\alpha - d}
* tau^2). So scaling tau by kappa^{\alpha-d/2} gives a parameter
that's proportional to 1/std.dev in the stationary case.
In the non-stationary case, the relationship is more complicated, but
similar. (there's a different model that has some more clear
theoretical underpinnings for decoupling variance and range, but it
doesn't fit in the spde2 implementation structure).

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] implement non-stationarity
parts:
No, B.tau = (*, 0 0 a, b), B.kappa = (* ,c, d, 0 0) does _not_
separate range and variance at all. For that, you need the range
parameters to also influence the tau construction;
something like
B.tau = cbind(*, +1, +values, -1, -values)
B.kappa = cbind(*, -1, -values, 0, 0)
based on equations 11 and 9 in the JSS paper. That lets theta1 and
theta2 control the log(range), and theta3 and theta4 control the
log(marginal standard deviation).

Finn

>>
>> The b_k(tau) = -b_k(kappa) part is needed if one wants to control the
>> range separately from the marginal variance. Both approaches give
>> "valid" models, but the interpretation and properties are different.
>> This is because in the basic (kappa^2 - Delta)^{alpha/2} (tau x) = W
>> model, the marginal variance is proportional to 1/(kappa^{2\alpha - d}
>> * tau^2). So scaling tau by kappa^{\alpha-d/2} gives a parameter
>> that's proportional to 1/std.dev in the stationary case.
>> In the non-stationary case, the relationship is more complicated, but
>> similar. (there's a different model that has some more clear
>> theoretical underpinnings for decoupling variance and range, but it
>> doesn't fit in the spde2 implementation structure).
>>

>> >> The internal representation is only theta_1=log(tau) when B.tau =
>> >> cbind(0, 1, 0); the internal representation is _defined_ by the
>> >> user-supplied B.tau and B.kappa matrices. Your representation is
>> >> precisely the intended way to extend this model to non-stationarity.
>> >> See the Details section of ?inla.spde2.matern, which defines the exact
>> >> construction. The inla.spde.result() method uses the B-matrices to
>> >> compute the nominal range and variance (or the log() of them) also in
>> >> the non-stationary case.
>> >> However, the tau&kappa parameterisation isn't the ideal way to
>> >> represent nonstationarity since it's hard to control the variance
>> >> behaviour (it depends on both kappa and tau), and there are several
>> >> solutions to this. One can be implemented using the existing
>> >> inla.spde2.matern function, but the best solution will require a new
>> >> internal model, that we're working on.
>> >>
>> >> For the inla.spde2.matern() interface, there is a better way to
>> >> parameterise the existing implementation to get at least partial
>> >> separation between range and variance; using the approach from the
>> >> 2015 JSS paper that uses "nominal range" and "nominal standard
>> >> deviation" as the basis for the parameterisation isn't perfect in the
>> >> non-stationary case, but it should be more well behaved than the pure
>> >> tau/kappa parameterisation. See pages 4-6 fo
>> >> https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v063i19 that includes the
>> >> derivation of the needed B.tau and B.kappa parameters.
>> >>
>> >> Of course, using a non-stationary extension of the PC-prior model for
>> >> the covariance parameters would be preferable, and that's part of what
>> >> one of my PhD students is currently working on.
